text: Welcome to Deep Learning and PyTorch, the first course in the AI and ML Research Engineer destination. Everything you'll build from here on is arithmetic on one data structure: the tensor. This lesson builds that foundation.

torch.tensor copies data you already have. zeros, ones, randn, and arange all take a shape and build a fresh tensor for you. The underscore-like variants, like zeros_like, copy another tensor's shape without you typing it out again. You'll reach for randn when you need random weights to start a model, and for zeros or ones when you need a known starting value.

Every tensor carries three facts you'll check constantly: its shape, the dimensions; its dtype, the element type like float32 or int64; and its device, whether the data lives on the CPU or a GPU. torch.float32 is the default for most operations, while torch.tensor on a list of whole numbers defaults to int64 instead. Mismatches in any of these three cause most of the errors you'll hit in PyTorch.

Indexing and slicing work like NumPy. A boolean mask, like a[a > 5], pulls out exactly the elements that satisfy a condition, without writing a single loop. Reshaping changes how a tensor's data is viewed. view requires the data to be contiguous in memory; reshape is the safer default because it falls back to copying. unsqueeze and squeeze add or remove size-one dimensions, which comes up constantly when matching a batch dimension.

Broadcasting lets elementwise operators like plus combine tensors of different but compatible shapes without a loop. Two shapes can broadcast whenever, compared from the right, each dimension either matches or one of them is a 1. Matrix multiplication follows a different rule entirely — the at symbol, or torch.matmul, is the operation underneath every linear layer you'll build starting in chapter two.

Shape, dtype, device — check those three first whenever something looks wrong. Up next, lesson two: autograd, where PyTorch starts tracking what you do to a tensor so it can compute gradients automatically.
